passage:
Come, Zeenat, sit. I'm Tanuja, and I want to tell you about my very first client, an old man named Mr. Bose who owned a print shop and believed in me when nobody else did. He gave me my first invoice.

Six years on, his business had grown into three cities. He wanted an online ordering system with payments and stock tracking. I knew how to make his brochures and his website. Not this.

I could have bluffed. I might have learned it on his money and let quality slip. But he had been so kind to me.

So I told him the truth. "I'm not the right person for this part. I'd like to help you find a proper team, and I'll keep looking after your brand work."

He was quiet, then said, "That is the honest thing." He still sends me his brochures. And the team I found is still with him.

qa.q: What kind of business did Mr. Bose own?
qa.a: Mr. Bose owned a print shop.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja not simply bluff and learn the new system on his money?
qa.a: Tanuja felt loyal and grateful to Mr. Bose, who had believed in Tanuja first, and did not want to let quality slip on a system beyond Tanuja's skills.

qa.q: What did Tanuja do that showed honest loyalty?
qa.a: Tanuja told Mr. Bose about the gap, offered to help him find a proper team and kept handling the brand work that Tanuja could do well.

qa.q: How might Mr. Bose have felt hearing that Tanuja could not do the system?
qa.a: Mr. Bose may have been disappointed at first, but his reply that it was the honest thing suggests he respected the truth over a false promise.

grounding: An early client's needs outgrow Tanuja; honest loyalty means naming the gap and helping them find better options.

passage:
Kalyani had been Imran's first client, three years ago, when his software shop in Aurangabad was a table in his uncle's garage. She ran a chain of three pharmacies then and gave him the billing system job when no one else would.
Now she had twelve stores and wanted an inventory system linked to her suppliers' systems, real-time, across two states. Imran read the brief twice and felt a knot in his stomach. His team of four had never built anything like it.
He could bluff. Say yes, learn on the way, hope. Kalyani trusted him.
Instead he drove to her head office. "Kalyani-madam, I owe you honesty. This is bigger than what we can build well. If I say yes, it'll be late and it'll break."
She frowned. "So what do I do?"
"I've spoken to two firms in Pune who do this. I'll help you evaluate them. And we'll keep maintaining your billing system."
She was quiet, then nodded. "That's why I trust you."

qa.q: How many stores does Kalyani have now?
What was Imran feeling when he read the new brief?
qa.a: He felt anxious and uneasy, a knot in his stomach, knowing his small team had never built anything like it.

qa.q: How did Imran show honest loyalty to Kalyani?
qa.a: He told her the job was beyond his team, recommended two firms that could do it, offered to help evaluate them, and kept supporting her billing system.

qa.q: How might Kalyani see Imran's honesty?
qa.a: Kalyani may be disappointed at first, but she trusts him more because he chose truth over bluffing.

grounding: An early client's needs outgrow the protagonist's ability; he tells her honestly about the gap and helps her find better options instead of bluffing.

passage:
"Darshan-ji, can we talk about the export order?"
"Preeti! Yes, the German buyer. You'll handle it, of course."
"That's what I need to talk about. Two hundred pieces a month, certified dyes, their audit. My workshop is eleven women and two looms."
"You'll manage. You always do."
"I wish. But I don't have the certification, and I can't get it in time. If I say yes, the quality will slip and you'll lose the buyer."
Darshan leaned back. "You were my first supplier. I stuck with you when your first batch was late."
"I know. That's why I'm being honest. I've spoken to a cooperative in Bhuj that has the certification. I can introduce you. I'd still like to do your local orders."
"You'd send me to someone else?"
"For this order, yes. It's better for you."
He was quiet for a while. "Set up the meeting."

qa.q: How many women work in Preeti's workshop?
What was Preeti feeling when Darshan said "You'll manage"?
qa.a: Preeti felt uneasy and pressured, worried the order couldn't be met without quality slipping.

qa.q: How did Preeti show honest loyalty to Darshan?
qa.a: Preeti told him about the gap in certification and capacity, and offered to introduce him to a certified cooperative in Bhuj while keeping his local orders.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel when Preeti suggests someone else?
qa.a: Darshan seems surprised and a little hurt, recalling his early loyalty, but comes to see the honesty as care for his business.

grounding: An early client's needs outgrow the protagonist's ability; the protagonist is honest about the gap and helps him find a better option rather than letting quality slip.
